apmo-2001-01.title: Count each digit's contribution
apmo-2001-01.body:
Write $n=a_k10^k+a_{k-1}10^{k-1}+\dots+a_110+a_0$ with digits $a_i$ and $a_k\ne0$. Removing the last $j$ digits ($1\le j\le k$) gives the stump
$$\left\lfloor \frac{n}{10^j}\right\rfloor=a_k10^{k-j}+a_{k-1}10^{k-1-j}+\dots+a_j ,$$
which is positive because its leading digit is $a_k\neq 0$; these are all the stumps (a one-digit $n$ has none, and then $T(n)=0$).

The digit $a_i$ appears in the stumps with $j=1,2,\dots,i$, with place values $10^{i-1},10^{i-2},\dots,10^0$. Hence
$$T(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}a_i\left(10^{i-1}+\dots+10+1\right)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}a_i\,\frac{10^i-1}{9}$$
(the empty sum for $i=0$ is $0=\frac{10^0-1}{9}$). Multiplying by $9$,
$$9T(n)=\sum_{i=0}^k a_i10^i-\sum_{i=0}^k a_i=n-S(n),$$
that is, $n=S(n)+9T(n)$. ∎

apmo-2001-01.title: Induction on the number of digits
apmo-2001-01.body:
For one-digit $n$ there are no stumps, $T(n)=0$ and $S(n)=n$, so the claim holds.

Suppose it holds for all numbers with $k$ digits and let $m$ have $k+1$ digits. Write $m=10n+a$ where $a$ is the last digit and $n$ has $k$ digits. The stumps of $m$ are $n$ itself and the stumps of $n$, so $T(m)=n+T(n)$; also $S(m)=S(n)+a$. Therefore
$$S(m)+9T(m)=S(n)+a+9n+9T(n)=\bigl(S(n)+9T(n)\bigr)+9n+a=n+9n+a=10n+a=m. \qquad ∎$$

apmo-2001-02.title: Bound $N$ with floor estimates
apmo-2001-02.body:
By inclusion–exclusion the condition is
$$\left\lfloor\frac N3\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac N5\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac N7\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac N{35}\right\rfloor .\tag{1}$$
Write $N=35k+r$ with $0\le r\le 34$. Since $35k$ is divisible by $5$, $7$ and $35$, the right side equals
$$7k+5k-k+\left\lfloor\frac r5\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac r7\right\rfloor=11k+\left\lfloor\frac r5\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac r7\right\rfloor\le 11k+\frac{12r}{35}.$$
The left side is at least $\frac{N-2}{3}=\frac{35k+r-2}{3}$. So (1) forces
$$\frac{35k+r-2}{3}\le 11k+\frac{12r}{35}\iff 1225k+35r-70\le 1155k+36r\iff 70k\le r+70\le 104 .$$
Hence $k\le1$ and $N\le 35+34=69$.

**Check $N=69,68,67,66,65$** ($k=1$, $r=N-35$):
- $N=69$: left $23$, right $11+6+4=21$.
- $N=68,67,66$: left $22$, right $11+6+4=21$.
- $N=65$: left $21$, right $11+\lfloor 30/5\rfloor+\lfloor30/7\rfloor=11+6+4=21$. ✓

Indeed, up to $65$ there are $21$ multiples of $3$, and $13+9-1=21$ numbers divisible by $5$ or $7$.

**Answer: $N=65$.**

apmo-2001-03.title: Alternation and similar corner triangles
apmo-2001-03.body:
Let $a$ be the side length and $\theta=\frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}$ the interior angle of both polygons. Orient everything counterclockwise.

**1. The sides of $S\cap T$ alternate in colour.** $S\cap T$ is a convex polygon; each of its sides lies on a side of $S$ or of $T$ and has the same outward normal direction as that side (because $S\cap T$ lies on the same side of the line as $S$, resp. $T$). A convex polygon has at most one side with a given outward normal. The normals of $S$ form the set $N_S=\{\varphi+2\pi k/n\}$, those of $T$ the set $N_T=\{\psi+2\pi k/n\}$. Since $S\cap T$ has $2n$ sides with distinct normals taken from $N_S\cup N_T$, we need $|N_S\cup N_T|=2n$, so $N_S\cap N_T=\emptyset$ and every side of $S$ and of $T$ carries exactly one side of $S\cap T$. Going around by increasing normal angle, exactly one element of $N_T$ lies strictly between two consecutive elements of $N_S$. So the sides of $S\cap T$ are alternately red and blue, and every vertex of $S\cap T$ is the intersection of a side of $S$ with a side of $T$.

**2. Corner triangles.** Let $A$ be a vertex of $S$ between the sides $s$ (incoming) and $s'$ (outgoing). The red sides on $s$ and $s'$ are consecutive red sides of $S\cap T$, so between them there is one blue side $DC$, with $D\in s$, $C\in s'$, lying on a side $t$ of $T$. If $D=A$, then $C$ and $D$ would both lie on the distinct lines $s'$ and $t$, forcing $C=D$, impossible; so $D\ne A$ and likewise $C\neq A$. Thus along side $s$ the order is: (start of red side), $D$, $A$; and $ADC$ is a genuine triangle with angle $\theta$ at $A$ and with base $DC$ = a blue side. Call it the corner triangle at $A$. In the same way each vertex $B$ of $T$ has a corner triangle whose apex angle is $\theta$ and whose base is a red side.

So there are $2n$ corner triangles, alternately at vertices of $S$ and of $T$ as we go around. Two consecutive ones share a vertex $D$ of $S\cap T$. If $D$ is the end of the red side $ED$ on $s$ and the start of the blue side $DC$ on $t$, the corner triangle at $A$ has angle $\angle ADC$ at $D$, while the corner triangle at the vertex $B$ of $T$ where $t$ starts is $BED$ with angle $\angle BDE$ at $D$. Since ray $DB$ is opposite to ray $DC$ and ray $DE$ is opposite to ray $DA$, these are vertical angles, so they are equal. Two triangles with apex angle $\theta$ and another common angle are similar; going around the cycle, **all $2n$ corner triangles are similar**, with the apex $\theta$ corresponding to the apex.

**3. Perimeters.** Fix a triangle with angles as above, base $u$ (opposite $\theta$) and legs $v,w$. The corner triangle at the $i$-th vertex of $S$ is this triangle scaled by some $p_i>0$, the one at the $i$-th vertex of $T$ is scaled by $q_i>0$. Let $P=\sum p_i$, $Q=\sum q_i$. The blue sides of $S\cap T$ are the bases of the $S$-corners, so their total is $uP$; likewise the red total is $uQ$.

Each side of $S$ consists of a leg of a corner triangle, a red side and a leg of the next corner triangle; over all sides every leg of every $S$-corner is used once. Hence
$$na=(v+w)P+uQ,\qquad\text{and similarly}\qquad na=(v+w)Q+uP .$$
Subtracting, $(v+w-u)(P-Q)=0$. By the triangle inequality $v+w>u$, so $P=Q$, i.e. the blue total $uP$ equals the red total $uQ$. ∎

apmo-2001-04.title: Rational coefficients, then an irrational preimage
apmo-2001-04.body:
The graph of $f$ has no mixed point iff: **$x\in\mathbb Q\Rightarrow f(x)\in\mathbb Q$, and $x\notin\mathbb Q\Rightarrow f(x)\notin\mathbb Q$.**

**Linear polynomials with rational coefficients work.** If $f(x)=ax+b$, $a,b\in\mathbb Q$, $a\ne0$: rational $x$ gives rational $f(x)$; if $x$ is irrational and $f(x)=y$ were rational, then $x=(y-b)/a$ would be rational. So no mixed points.

**Constants fail:** if $f\equiv c$ with $c$ rational, $(\sqrt2,c)$ is mixed; if $c$ is irrational, $(0,c)$ is mixed.

**The coefficients must be rational.** Let $d=\deg f\ge1$. Take rational $r_0,\dots,r_d$ (distinct); the values $f(r_i)$ are rational. The Lagrange interpolation polynomial
$$g(x)=\sum_{i=0}^d f(r_i)\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{x-r_j}{r_i-r_j}$$
has rational coefficients and agrees with $f$ at $d+1$ points; since $f-g$ has degree $\le d$ and $d+1$ roots, $f=g$.

**Degree $d\ge2$ fails.** Choose a positive integer $M$ such that $g=Mf$ has integer coefficients; replacing $f$ by $-f$ if necessary (this does not change the property), the leading coefficient $A$ of $g$ is a positive integer. For any integer $m$, if a rational $y=u/v$ (lowest terms) satisfies $g(y)=m$, then by the rational root theorem applied to $g(x)-m$ we get $v\mid A$, so $y$ is a multiple of $\frac1A$.

The difference $g\left(x+\frac1A\right)-g(x)$ is a polynomial in $x$ of degree $d-1\ge1$ with leading coefficient $A\cdot d\cdot\frac1A=d>0$, so it exceeds $1$ for all $x\ge X_0$. Pick an integer $k$ with $\frac kA\ge X_0$. Then $g\left(\frac{k+1}{A}\right)-g\left(\frac kA\right)>1$, so some integer $m$ lies strictly between these two values, and by the intermediate value theorem $g(y)=m$ for some $y$ strictly between $\frac kA$ and $\frac{k+1}A$. This $y$ is not a multiple of $\frac1A$, hence irrational, while $f(y)=\frac mM$ is rational: $(y,f(y))$ is a mixed point.

**Answer:** exactly the polynomials $f(x)=ax+b$ with $a,b$ rational and $a\neq0$. ∎

apmo-2001-05.title: Four types of points, paired up
apmo-2001-05.body:
"Equal" means congruent. Let $a=AB$, $c=CD$, $a\ne c$.

**Types.** For $X=X_i$ the triangles $ABX$ and $CDX$ have the same multiset of side lengths: $\{a,AX,BX\}=\{c,CX,DX\}$. Since $a\ne c$, $a$ must equal $CX$ or $DX$, and $c$ must equal $AX$ or $BX$. Say $X$ has **type $(P,Q)$** ($P\in\{A,B\}$, $Q\in\{C,D\}$) if $PX=c$ and $QX=a$. Removing these from the multisets leaves $P'X=Q'X$, where $P'$, $Q'$ are the other points of $\{A,B\}$, $\{C,D\}$. So:
- type $(B,C)$: $BX=c$, $CX=a$, $AX=DX$; type $(A,D)$: $AX=c$, $DX=a$, $BX=CX$;
- type $(A,C)$: $AX=c$, $CX=a$, $BX=DX$; type $(B,D)$: $BX=c$, $DX=a$, $AX=CX$.

A point of type $(P,Q)$ lies on the circle with centre $P$, radius $c$ and on the circle with centre $Q$, radius $a$; two circles with distinct centres meet in at most $2$ points. So each type has at most $2$ points (and $n\le8$).

**Claim: types $(B,C)$ and $(A,D)$ together contain at most $2$ of the $X_i$.** Otherwise one type has $2$ points and the other at least $1$. Relabelling $A\leftrightarrow B$, $C\leftrightarrow D$ swaps these two types and keeps $AB$, $CD$, so we may assume type $(B,C)$ contains $X_1\ne X_2$ and type $(A,D)$ contains $Y$.

$X_1,X_2$ are the two common points of circles centred at $B$ and $C$, so $X_1X_2\perp BC$; both lie on the perpendicular bisector $m$ of $AD$ (as $AX=DX$), so $X_1X_2=m$. Hence $AD\perp m$ and $BC\perp m$. Take coordinates with $m$ as the $y$-axis:
$$A=(-s,\alpha),\ D=(s,\alpha),\ B=(b,\beta),\ C=(e,\beta),\ X_1=(0,y_1),$$
with $b\ne e$. The point $Y$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, the line $x=\frac{b+e}2$. Put $K=c^2-a^2\neq0$. Then
- $BX_1^2-CX_1^2=c^2-a^2$ gives $b^2-e^2=K$;
- $AY^2-DY^2=c^2-a^2$ gives $\left(\frac{b+e}2+s\right)^2-\left(\frac{b+e}2-s\right)^2=2s(b+e)=K$;
- directly, $K=CD^2-AB^2=\bigl[(s-e)^2+h^2\bigr]-\bigl[(b+s)^2+h^2\bigr]=(e^2-b^2)-2s(b+e)$, where $h=\alpha-\beta$.

The last line gives $K=-K-K=-2K$, so $K=0$, a contradiction. This proves the claim.

Relabelling $C\leftrightarrow D$ turns types $(A,C),(B,D)$ into $(A,D),(B,C)$, so types $(A,C)$ and $(B,D)$ also contain at most $2$ points together. Every $X_i$ has at least one type, so $n\le 4$.

**An example with $n=4$.** Take
$$A=(0,0),\ B=(1,\sqrt3),\ C=(1,-\sqrt3),\ D=(3,\sqrt3),$$
so $AB=2\ne4=CD$, and
$$X_1=(2,-2\sqrt3),\ X_2=(3,-\sqrt3),\ X_3=(4,0),\ X_4=(5,\sqrt3).$$
The side lengths $(AX,BX;\ CX,DX)$ are $(4,\sqrt{28};\,2,\sqrt{28})$, $(\sqrt{12},4;\,2,\sqrt{12})$, $(4,\sqrt{12};\,\sqrt{12},2)$, $(\sqrt{28},4;\,\sqrt{28},2)$. In each case $\{2,AX,BX\}=\{4,CX,DX\}$, and none of the $X_i$ lies on line $AB$ ($y=\sqrt3x$) or line $CD$ ($y=\sqrt3(x-2)$), so all eight triangles are genuine and $ABX_i\cong CDX_i$.

**Answer: $n=4$.**
